Group 6

Spine

Who arrives in acute coronary crisis, which habits travel with that crisis, and where in Africa is life short?

This sentence stays at the top. Every panel must attach to it.

Introduction — the tables we own

This folder is ours for the ten days. Our tables, our shapes.

  • Panel A (panel-A.csv) — acute coronary syndrome patients: age, BMI, cholesterol (TC, LDLC, HDLC) and EF, plus sex and obesity.
  • Panel B (panel-B.csv) — same patients, Quals: smoking, sex, DM, HBP, Dx, cardiogenic shock.
  • Panel C (panel-C.csv) — gapminder 2007. Join by country name.
  • Panel D — Erin Brockovich in Hinkley: a hand-built plume and family homes.
  • Panel E — Found Data: six campus hunches we collected ourselves (AI belief, allowance, MBTI, relationships, tattoos, TV shows).
library(tidyverse)
library(mosaic)
library(skimr)
library(ggformula)
##
library(broom) # for clean stat outputs
library(sf) # for Panel-C
library(rnaturalearth) # for Panel-C
library(leaflet) # for Panel-D
library(readxl) # for Hunch 6
library(janitor) # for Hunch 3 and Hunch 6
# vcd and supernova must be installed, but we do NOT load them with library().
# We always write vcd::mosaic() and supernova::supernova(), so vcd's mosaic()
# never fights with the mosaic package.

A <- read_csv("data/panel-A.csv")
B <- read_csv("data/panel-B.csv")
C <- read_csv("data2/panel-C.csv")

Found tables train the mark. A campus Free Hunch is a made panel of the same pair type.

2. Ask

One question this table can answer. One it cannot. Write both.

Looking at the overall Spine statement, I can pose the following Questions:

Possibly can answer:

  1. Are people with more BMI prone to becoming obese?
  2. Is obesity impacted by age? (Main Character Question)
  3. Is the age and obesity pattern different for men and women?
  4. Is TC associated with LDLC?
  5. Does cholesterol (TC) increase with age?
  6. How do HDLC and LDLC vary in the population?

Possibly cannot answer:

  1. Does EF increase or decrease with BMI? (The data doesn’t show the relation between EF and BMI properly)
  2. How much fat can a person with a given HDLC eat and keep a stable EF? (No diet data)
  3. Does more workout lead to increased EF? (No exercise data)
  4. How many people whose EF changed with LDLC have died? (No follow-up or death data)

3. Choose a mark

Geom, map mark, or (later) test that matches the pair type. Name it before you code.

  1. Box plot + Stat Test For Means
  2. Histograms, coloured by obesity + Stat Test For Means
  3. Box plot, coloured by sex
  4. Scatter Plot + Correlation Test
  5. Scatter Plot, coloured by sex + Correlation Test
  6. Histograms

4. Predict

What do we think we will see? One sentence, before Run.

  1. I think obese patients will have a much higher BMI.
  2. I think obese patients will be younger on average than non-obese patients.
  3. I think the pattern will look similar for men and women.
  4. I think TC and LDLC will be strongly positively correlated, since LDLC is part of TC.
  5. I think TC will go up a little with age.
  6. I think LDLC will be spread much wider than HDLC.

Human brick first. Optional: one AI prompt, pasted below, only for what section 3 named.

6. Say

Caption + one sentence we will stand behind.

  1. Obese patients have a clearly higher BMI (mean ___ vs , p-value ). No surprise, since obesity is decided from BMI in the first place. (fill in from the Question 1 output)
  2. The mean age of obese and non-obese patients differs by ___ years (p-value ___). (fill in from the t-test table: if p < 0.05 the difference is significant, if not, age does not clearly change obesity)
  3. The age and obesity pattern looks ___ for men and women. (fill in from the Question 3 box plot)
  4. TC and LDLC are positively correlated (r = , p-value ). (fill in from the Question 4 output)
  5. TC ___ with age (r = , p-value ). (fill in from the Question 5 output)
  6. HDLC is ___ and LDLC is ___. (fill in the shape and spread from the Question 6 histograms)

7. Limit

What this panel cannot do.

  • It cannot say why people become obese or why cholesterol rises (no diet, exercise or family history data).
  • It only has patients who already arrived in acute coronary crisis, so it cannot speak for healthy people.
  • It is one snapshot, so it cannot show change over TIME.
  • Correlation is not causation: TC and LDLC moving together does not mean one causes the other.

2. Ask

One question this table can answer. One it cannot. Write both.

Looking at the spine statement again, I can pose the following Questions:

Possibly can answer:

  1. Does obesity differ between males and females, more than we would expect by chance? (Main Character Question)
  2. Does smoking status differ across STEMI, NSTEMI, and Unstable Angina patients?
  3. Is obesity distributed differently across the different diagnosis (Dx) groups?
  4. Is cardiogenicShock more common in certain Dx groups?
  5. Does the type of entry, Radial or Femoral, differ across Dx groups?

Possibly cannot answer:

  1. Does smoking cause STEMI? (Patients were not assigned to smoke. This is not an RCT.)
  2. How many cigarettes a day is risky? (No amount of smoking, only a category)

3. Choose a mark

Geom, map mark, or (later) test that matches the pair type. Name it before you code.

  1. Mosaic Chart + Chi-Square Test
  2. Bar Chart with fill, dodged
  3. Bar Chart with fill, as proportions
  4. Mosaic Chart
  5. Bar Chart with fill, dodged

4. Predict

What do we think we will see? One sentence, before Run.

  1. I think obesity will be about the same for men and women, so the chi-square test will not be significant.
  2. I think smokers will show up most among STEMI patients.
  3. I think obesity will look similar across the Dx groups.
  4. I think cardiogenic shock will be most common in STEMI.
  5. I think entry will look similar across the Dx groups.

5. Make

Human brick first. Optional: one AI prompt, pasted below, only for what section 3 named.

# Question 1 (Main Character)
B_table <- vcd::structable(obesity ~ sex, data = B_mod)
B_table
       obesity  No Yes
sex                   
Female         194  93
Male           373 197
vcd::mosaic(B_table, shade = TRUE, main = "Does obesity differ between males and females?")
vcd::mosaic(B_table, type = "expected", main = "What would we expect by chance?")
# Question 2
B_mod |> gf_bar(~ Dx, fill = ~ smoking, position = "dodge", title = "Does smoking status differ across STEMI, NSTEMI, and Unstable Angina patients?")
# Question 3
B_mod |> gf_bar(~ Dx, fill = ~ obesity, position = "fill", title = "Is obesity distributed differently across the diagnosis groups?")
# Question 4
vcd::structable(cardiogenicShock ~ Dx, data = B_mod) |>
  vcd::mosaic(shade = TRUE, main = "Is cardiogenic shock more common in certain diagnosis groups?")
# Question 5
B_mod |> gf_bar(~ Dx, fill = ~ entry, position = "dodge", title = "Does the type of entry, Radial or Femoral, differ across diagnosis groups?")

6. Say

Caption + one sentence we will stand behind.

  1. Obesity ___ differ between men and women (X-squared = , p-value ). (fill in from the chi-square output: if p < 0.05 it does differ, if not, it does not)
  2. Smokers are ___ among STEMI patients compared to NSTEMI and Unstable Angina. (fill in from the Question 2 bar chart)
  3. The share of obese patients looks ___ across the Dx groups. (fill in from the Question 3 bar chart)
  4. Cardiogenic shock is most common in ___. (fill in from the coloured tiles in the Question 4 mosaic)
  5. entry looks ___ across the Dx groups. (fill in from the Question 5 bar chart)

7. Limit

What this panel cannot do.

  • It cannot say that smoking or obesity causes a diagnosis. Nobody was assigned to smoke, so this is not an RCT.
  • It only has patients who already arrived in acute coronary crisis, so it cannot speak for healthy people.
  • It has categories only, so it cannot say how much smoking or weight is risky.

$ geometry   <MULTIPOLYGON [°]> MULTIPOLYGON (((31.28789 -2..., MULTIPOLYGON (…

world is an sf data frame, with a MULTIPOLYGON geometry column, which we need. The name column has the name of the country, which is what we will use to join with our Panel-C data.

Let us select just the name and geometry columns first, and then join with Panel-C data. In passing, we will also mutate country and continent into factors.

NOTE: the join fails for two countries, because the names are spelled differently. Panel-C says “United States” and “Dominican Republic”, while world says “United States of America” and “Dominican Rep.”. We fix the names in Panel-C before joining.

world_selected <- world |> dplyr::select(name, geometry)

C_mod <- C |>
  ###
  mutate(country = case_when(
    country == "United States" ~ "United States of America",
    country == "Dominican Republic" ~ "Dominican Rep.",
    .default = country
  )) |>
  ###
  left_join(world_selected, by = c("country" = "name")) |>
  ###
  mutate(
    country = as_factor(country),
    continent = as_factor(continent)
  ) |>
  ###
  st_as_sf() # left_join() on a tibble drops the sf class, so put it back

glimpse(C_mod)

Finally, after joining, on the Qual variables Panel-C data has:

  • country: Qualitative, categorical. Encoded with 25 levels, one per country, from “Argentina” to “Venezuela”.
  • continent: Qualitative, categorical. Encoded with 1 level: “Americas”

And the Quant variables are:

  • year: Quantitative, numeric. One value only: 2007
  • lifeExp: Quantitative, numeric. Mean: 73.6, sd: 4.44, min: 60.9, median: 72.9, max: 80.7
  • pop: Quantitative, numeric. Mean: 3.60e+07, sd: 6.88e+07, min: 1.06e+06, median: 9.32e+06, max: 3.01e+08
  • gdpPercap: Quantitative, numeric. Mean: 11003, sd: 9713, min: 1202, median: 8948, max: 42952

There is no missing data. pop and gdpPercap are extremely right-skewed, which is why we use log scales below.

2. Ask

One question this table can answer. One it cannot. Write both.

Possibly can answer:

  1. How is pop spread across the countries of the Americas?
  2. How does gdpPercap vary per country across the Americas? (Main Character Question)
  3. Are gdpPercap and lifeExp related?
  4. Where on the map are the high pop, lifeExp and gdpPercap countries?

Possibly cannot answer:

  1. Why are some countries richer than others? (No data on causes)
  2. Do the quant variables change over time? (Only one year)

3. Choose a mark

Geom, map mark, or (later) test that matches the pair type. Name it before you code.

  1. Bar chart (gf_col) for pop per country
  2. Violin + jitter, and Box + jitter, for gdpPercap
  3. Scatter plot for lifeExp vs gdpPercap + Correlation Test
  4. Maps (gf_sf)

4. Predict

What do we think we will see? One sentence, before Run.

I think more populous countries have higher gdp per capita and that richer countries will have higher lifeExp.

5. Make

Human brick first. Optional: one AI prompt, pasted below, only for what section 3 named.

# Question 1
C_mod |>
  gf_col(reorder(country, pop) ~ pop, fill = ~ continent,
         title = "How is population spread across the countries of the Americas?") |>
  gf_labs(y = "country") |>
  gf_refine(scale_x_log10())
# Question 2
ggplot(C_mod, aes(continent, gdpPercap, colour = continent)) +
  geom_violin() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(title = "How does GDP per capita vary per country across the Americas?")
# Question 2
ggplot(C_mod, aes(continent, gdpPercap, colour = continent)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(title = "How does GDP per capita vary per country across the Americas?")
# Question 3
ggplot(C_mod, aes(gdpPercap, lifeExp, colour = continent)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() + # decompress the points squashed on the left of the graph
  labs(title = "Are GDP per capita and life expectancy related?")
mosaic::cor.test(lifeExp ~ gdpPercap, data = C_mod) |> broom::tidy()
# A tibble: 1 × 8
  estimate statistic  p.value parameter conf.low conf.high method    alternative
     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <int>    <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>     <chr>      
1    0.679      10.9 1.69e-20       140    0.579     0.759 Pearson'… two.sided  
# Question 4
C_mod |> gf_sf(geometry = ~ geometry, fill = ~ pop, color = ~ continent,
        title = "Where do the most people live in the Americas?")
C_mod |> gf_sf(geometry = ~ geometry, fill = ~ lifeExp, color = ~ continent,
        title = "Where is life expectancy highest in the Americas?")
C_mod |> gf_sf(geometry = ~ geometry, fill = ~ gdpPercap, color = ~ continent,
        title = "Where is GDP per capita highest in the Americas?")

6. Say

Caption + one sentence we will stand behind.

  1. Population is very uneven: the United States (about 301 million) and Brazil (about 190 million) are far bigger than everyone else, while the middle country has only about 9.3 million people.
  2. Most countries of the Americas sit between about 5,700 and 12,000 dollars of gdpPercap. The box plot alone hides the story, but the jitter shows two countries far above the rest, the United States (42,952) and Canada (36,319), and one far below, Haiti (1,202).
  3. Across the 25 countries of the Americas, lifeExp and gdpPercap are positively correlated (r = 0.59, p-value = 0.002). Haiti is the poorest country and also has the shortest life, at 60.9 years.
  4. On the maps, the richest and longest-living countries are in the north (Canada and the United States). Our prediction was only half right: the biggest country is also the richest, but Brazil, the second biggest, is only in the middle for gdpPercap.

7. Limit

What this panel cannot do.

  • It doesn’t say why countries differ.
  • It doesn’t show change over TIME, since there is only 2007.
  • It doesn’t prove that money causes long life. Correlation is not causation.
  • It only covers the Americas, so it cannot answer the “where in Africa” part of our spine.

Panel D — Erin Brockovich

Erin Brockovich in Hinkley, California: a hand-built plume of contaminated water and the homes of the families she met.

1. See the table

What is a case? Which columns are Quant / Qual? What is missing?

First, a base map pointed at Hinkley, so we can check we are in the right place. Esri.WorldImagery is satellite, so the PG&E site, streets and houses show up at zoom 14.

leaflet() |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldImagery") |>
  setView(lng = -117.2050, lat = 34.9360, zoom = 14)

Tibble #1: the plume. Each row is one corner of the plume POLYGON. It starts at the PG&E tanks and runs about 1 mile southwards towards Hinkley.

plume <- tibble(
  lng = c(-117.2135, -117.2095, -117.2040, -117.2030, -117.2090, -117.2160, -117.2165),
  lat = c( 34.9460,   34.9460,   34.9380,   34.9270,   34.9230,   34.9290,   34.9390)
)

My data has:

  • plume: 7 rows and 2 columns. Each row is one corner of the plume.
  • families: 5 rows and 11 columns. Each row is one family’s home.
  • family, address, phone: Qualitative, categorical. Encoded . One per family.
  • illness: Qualitative, categorical. Encoded
  • severity: Qualitative, ordinal (“Low” < “Medium” < “High”). Encoded
  • water_from: Qualitative, categorical. Encoded . Every family drinks well water.
  • signed_up: Qualitative, categorical (“Yes” / “No”). Did the family join the case against PG&E?
  • col: the colour for each severity, used to colour the markers.
  • people: Quantitative, numeric. How many people live in the home.
  • lng, lat: Quantitative, numeric. Where the point is.

There is no missing data. Everything is made up by hand: the families, addresses, phone numbers and illnesses are hypothetical, and the coordinates are approximate.

2. Ask

One question this table can answer. One it cannot. Write both.

Possibly can answer:

  1. Which families live on top of the plume, and how sick are they? (Main Character Question)

Possibly cannot answer:

  1. Did the chromium in the water cause the illnesses? (No water tests or medical records)
  2. How did the plume grow over the years? (One snapshot only)

3. Choose a mark

Geom, map mark, or (later) test that matches the pair type. Name it before you code.

  1. Interactive map (leaflet): plume as addPolygons(), homes as addCircleMarkers() coloured by severity, with popups and a legend

4. Predict

What do we think we will see? One sentence, before Run.

I think the families closest to the PG&E tanks, in the middle of the plume, will have the most severe illnesses.

5. Make

Human brick first. Optional: one AI prompt, pasted below, only for what section 3 named.

Which families live on top of the plume, and how sick are they?

# Question 1
popup <- paste(
  "<strong>", families$family, "</strong><br>",
  families$address, "<br>",
  "Phone: ", families$phone, "<br>",
  "People at home: ", families$people, "<br>",
  "Illness: ", families$illness, "<br>",
  "Severity: ", families$severity, "<br>",
  "Water from: ", families$water_from, "<br>",
  "Signed up: ", families$signed_up, "<br>"
)

leaflet(data = families) |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldImagery") |>
  setView(lng = -117.2050, lat = 34.9360, zoom = 14) |>
  # Tibble #1: the plume
  addPolygons(
    lng = plume$lng, lat = plume$lat,
    color = "purple", weight = 2,
    fill = TRUE, fillColor = "purple",
    popup = "Contaminated groundwater plume"
  ) |>
  # The PG&E tanks
  addMarkers(
    lng = -117.2115, lat = 34.9455,
    label = "PG&E compressor station (tanks)",
    labelOptions = labelOptions(noHide = TRUE, textOnly = FALSE, textsize = 14)
  ) |>
  # Tibble #2: the families, coloured by severity
  addCircleMarkers(
    lng = ~lng, lat = ~lat,
    radius = 8, # Pixels
    color = families$col,
    stroke = FALSE,
    fillOpacity = 1,
    label = families$family,
    popup = popup
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    title = "Illness severity",
    colors = c("red", "orange", "yellow"),
    labels = c("High", "Medium", "Low")
  )

6. Say

Caption + one sentence we will stand behind.

Every family on the map lives on top of the plume and drinks well water. The two families closest to the PG&E tanks, the Jensens and the Robinsons, have the most severe illnesses, while the Matthews family, at the far southern tip of the plume, has the mildest.

7. Limit

What this panel cannot do.

  • It isn’t proof that the chromium caused the illnesses.
  • It doesn’t speak for the whole town (only 5 made-up families).
  • It doesn’t show how the plume spread over TIME.

2. Ask

One question this table can answer. One it cannot. Write both.

Possibly can answer:

  1. Do design students have greater belief in AI compared to art students? (Main Character Question)
  2. Does it differ between boys and girls?

Possibly cannot answer:

  1. Why do students believe in AI or not? (We only asked yes / no)

3. Choose a mark

Geom, map mark, or (later) test that matches the pair type. Name it before you code.

  1. Mosaic Chart + Chi-Square Test

4. Predict

What do we think we will see? One sentence, before Run.

We think Design students are more likely to have a greater belief in AI compared to art students, and boys are more likely to have a greater belief than girls.

5. Make

Human brick first. Optional: one AI prompt, pasted below, only for what section 3 named.

# Question 1 and 2
vcd::structable(AI_belief ~ program + gender, data = AI) |>
  vcd::mosaic(shade = TRUE, main = "Do design students believe in AI more than art students? Boys more than girls?")

6. Say

Caption + one sentence we will stand behind.

Gender, not program, drives AI belief.

  1. Design students said yes a little more often than art students (16 of 30 vs 12 of 30), but the difference is not significant (X-squared = 0.60, p-value = 0.44).
  2. Boys believe significantly more than girls (19 of 30 boys vs 9 of 30 girls said yes, X-squared = 5.42, p-value = 0.02), regardless of whether they study art or design.

7. Limit

What this panel cannot do.

“Belief” means something different to each student. One person might say yes because AI exists and they use it daily; another might say no because they’re thinking about ethics or environmental cost.

Possibly cannot answer:

  1. Why are some students in a relationship and others not? (We only asked yes / no)

Geom, map mark, or (later) test that matches the pair type. Name it before you code.

  1. Bar chart as proportions, Mosaic Chart + Chi-Square Test

4. Predict

What do we think we will see? One sentence, before Run.

SMI students are more likely to be in a relationship (or a situationship) than MIT students.

Human brick first. Optional: one AI prompt, pasted below, only for what section 3 named.

  vcd::mosaic(shade = TRUE, main = "Relationship status by department")

6. Say

Caption + one sentence we will stand behind.

The romantic art student is a myth, at least on our campus.

12 SMI students and 13 MIT students said yes, almost identical. The test confirms there is no real difference (p = 1).

7. Limit

What this panel cannot do.

A one-person difference between 12 and 13 means nothing statistically. “Relationship” was also left undefined, so some students may have counted situationships and others may not.

My h6 data has:

  • students: Quantitative, numeric. Just the student’s number.
  • friends, house, modern_family: each student’s score for that show. Excel stored the scores as dates , so the score is hiding in the day of the date. We pull it out with lubridate::day().

Then we pivot_longer() the three show columns into two: show (Qual) and scores (Quant), so that each row is one student’s score for one show.

h6_mod <- h6 |>
  mutate(
    friends = lubridate::day(friends) |> as.numeric(),
    house = lubridate::day(house) |> as.numeric(),
    modern_family = lubridate::day(modern_family) |> as.numeric()
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(-students), names_to = "show", values_to = "scores") |>
  mutate(show = as.factor(show))

  1. Which show do students rate highest: Friends, House or Modern Family? (Main Character Question)
  2. Which pairs of shows are rated differently?

Possibly cannot answer:

  1. Why do students like one show more than another? (We only have a score)

3. Choose a mark

Geom, map mark, or (later) test that matches the pair type. Name it before you code.

  1. Density plot, Box Plot + ANOVA
  2. Pairwise comparison plot

4. Predict

What do we think we will see? One sentence, before Run.

Modern Family will be rated the highest of the three shows.

5. Make

Human brick first. Optional: one AI prompt, pasted below, only for what section 3 named.

# Question 1
tvshows_clean |> gf_density(~ scores, fill = ~ show, alpha = 0.5, title = "Which show do students rate highest?")
tvshows_clean |> gf_boxplot(scores ~ show, fill = ~ show, title = "Which show do students rate highest?")
# Question 2
aov(scores ~ show, data = tvshows_clean) |> supernova::pairwise(plot = TRUE)
── Tukey's Honestly Significant Differences ────────────────────────────────────
Model: scores ~ show
show
Levels: 3

  <chr>         <chr>    <dbl>     <dbl>  <dbl> <int>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 house         friends -0.674     0.270 -2.495   136 -1.579 0.231 .1855
2 modern_family friends  0.859     0.231  3.710   136  0.083 1.634 .0261
3 modern_family house    1.533     0.272  5.637   136  0.621 2.444 .0003

6. Say

Caption + one sentence we will stand behind.

Modern Family was rated the highest overall, as we predicted, with ratings clustering around 8-9, while House had the most spread with people either loving it or not. The ANOVA confirms these differences are real and not just chance (F = 8.44, p = 0.0004).

The pairwise comparison further revealed that Modern Family was rated significantly higher than both Friends and House. However, there was no statistically significant difference between Friends and House.

This suggests that Modern Family was the clear favourite among the students who rated these shows, supporting our hunch.

7. Limit

What this panel cannot do.

In this dataset, there were a lot of missing values (NA), since not many people had watched/rated House. In an ideal study, all the people within the sample should have watched all the shows, Friends, House and Modern Family.

Conclusion

  • The question we will defend in ninety seconds: Who arrives in acute coronary crisis, which habits travel with that crisis, and where is life short? Panels A and B answer the first two with the patients’ bodies and habits, and Panel C shows that in the Americas, richer countries live longer (r = 0.59).
  • What we will not claim: that smoking, obesity or cholesterol cause a crisis, that money causes long life, or that chromium caused the illnesses in Hinkley. Nothing here was an experiment.
  • Limits: one snapshot in time, patients who already arrived in crisis, the Americas instead of Africa in Panel C, made-up families in Panel D, and small, self-reported campus samples (n = 60 to 69) in Panel E.

# Spine

> Who arrives in acute coronary crisis, which habits travel with that crisis, and where in Africa is life short?

~~This sentence stays at the top. Every panel must attach to it.~~

# Introduction — the tables we own

This folder is ours for the ten days. Our tables, our shapes.

- **Panel A** (`panel-A.csv`) — acute coronary syndrome patients: age, BMI, cholesterol (TC, LDLC, HDLC) and EF, plus sex and obesity.
- **Panel B** (`panel-B.csv`) — same patients, Quals: smoking, sex, DM, HBP, Dx, cardiogenic shock.
- **Panel C** (`panel-C.csv`) — gapminder 2007. Join by country name.
- **Panel D** — Erin Brockovich in Hinkley: a hand-built plume and family homes.
- **Panel E** — Found Data: six campus hunches we collected ourselves (AI belief, allowance, MBTI, relationships, tattoos, TV shows).

```{r}
#| label: FOSEDA
#| message: false # keeps rendered Quarto less noisy
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)
library(mosaic)
library(skimr)
library(ggformula)
##
library(broom) # for clean stat outputs
library(sf) # for Panel-C
library(rnaturalearth) # for Panel-C
library(leaflet) # for Panel-D
library(readxl) # for Hunch 6
library(janitor) # for Hunch 3 and Hunch 6
# vcd and supernova must be installed, but we do NOT load them with library().
# We always write vcd::mosaic() and supernova::supernova(), so vcd's mosaic()
# never fights with the mosaic package.

A <- read_csv("data/panel-A.csv")
B <- read_csv("data/panel-B.csv")
C <- read_csv("data2/panel-C.csv")
```

### 7. Limit

~~What this panel cannot do.~~

- It cannot say *why* people become obese or why cholesterol rises (no diet, exercise or family history data).
- It only has patients who already arrived in acute coronary crisis, so it cannot speak for healthy people.
- It is one snapshot, so it cannot show change over TIME.
- Correlation is not causation: `TC` and `LDLC` moving together does not mean one causes the other.

# Panel C — place

*lifeExp / gdpPercap / pop by country and continent. Same join brick as other map panels.*

### 1. See the table

~~What is a case? Which columns are Quant / Qual? What is missing?~~

```{r}
#| label: inspect-panel-C-data-1

dplyr::glimpse(C)
```

My Panel-C data has:

- 25 rows and 6 columns. Each row (case) is one country of the Americas in 2007.
- `country`: Qualitative, categorical. Encoded <chr>, to be mutated
- `continent`: Qualitative, categorical. Encoded <chr>, to be mutated
- `year`: Quantitative, numeric. It is 2007 all the way down, so the data is for one year only.
- `lifeExp`: Quantitative, numeric
- `pop`: Quantitative, numeric
- `gdpPercap`: Quantitative, numeric

Let us `join` this data with map geometries from `rnaturalearth`, so that we can make maps of the quant variables.

```{r}
#| label: get-map-data

world <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf")
glimpse(world)
```

`world` is an `sf` data frame, with a MULTIPOLYGON `geometry` column, which we need. The `name` column has the name of the country, which is what we will use to `join` with our Panel-C data.

Let us select just the `name` and `geometry` columns first, and then join with Panel-C data. In passing, we will also mutate `country` and `continent` into factors.

NOTE: the join fails for two countries, because the names are spelled differently. Panel-C says "United States" and "Dominican Republic", while `world` says "United States of America" and "Dominican Rep.". We fix the names in Panel-C before joining.

```{r}
#| label: join-data

world_selected <- world |> dplyr::select(name, geometry)

C_mod <- C |>
  ###
  mutate(country = case_when(
    country == "United States" ~ "United States of America",
    country == "Dominican Republic" ~ "Dominican Rep.",
    .default = country
  )) |>
  ###
  left_join(world_selected, by = c("country" = "name")) |>
  ###
  mutate(
    country = as_factor(country),
    continent = as_factor(continent)
  ) |>
  ###
  st_as_sf() # left_join() on a tibble drops the sf class, so put it back

glimpse(C_mod)
```

```{r}
#| label: inspect-panel-C-data-2

C_mod |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |> # skim() cannot summarise the map shapes, so drop them here only
  skimr::skim()
```

Finally, after joining, on the Qual variables Panel-C data has:

- `country`: Qualitative, categorical. Encoded <fct> with 25 levels, one per country, from "Argentina" to "Venezuela".
- `continent`: Qualitative, categorical. Encoded <fct> with 1 level: "Americas"

And the Quant variables are:

- `year`: Quantitative, numeric. One value only: 2007
- `lifeExp`: Quantitative, numeric. Mean: 73.6, sd: 4.44, min: 60.9, median: 72.9, max: 80.7
- `pop`: Quantitative, numeric. Mean: 3.60e+07, sd: 6.88e+07, min: 1.06e+06, median: 9.32e+06, max: 3.01e+08
- `gdpPercap`: Quantitative, numeric. Mean: 11003, sd: 9713, min: 1202, median: 8948, max: 42952

There is no missing data. `pop` and `gdpPercap` are extremely right-skewed, which is why we use log scales below.

### 2. Ask

~~One question *this* table can answer. One it cannot. Write both.~~

Possibly can answer:

1. How is `pop` spread across the countries of the Americas?
1. How does `gdpPercap` vary per country across the Americas? (Main Character Question)
1. Are `gdpPercap` and `lifeExp` related?
1. Where on the map are the high `pop`, `lifeExp` and `gdpPercap` countries?

Possibly cannot answer:

1. Why are some countries richer than others? (No data on causes)
1. Do the quant variables change over time? (Only one `year`)

### 3. Choose a mark

~~Geom, map mark, or (later) test that matches the pair type. Name it before you code.~~

1. Bar chart (`gf_col`) for `pop` per country
1. Violin + jitter, and Box + jitter, for `gdpPercap`
1. Scatter plot for `lifeExp` vs `gdpPercap` + Correlation Test
1. Maps (`gf_sf`)

### 4. Predict

~~What do we think we will see? One sentence, before Run.~~

I think more populous countries have higher gdp per capita and that richer countries will have higher `lifeExp`.

### 5. Make

~~Human brick first. Optional: one AI prompt, pasted below, only for what section 3 named.~~

```{r}
#| label: question-1-pop-per-country
#| warning: false

# Question 1
C_mod |>
  gf_col(reorder(country, pop) ~ pop, fill = ~ continent,
         title = "How is population spread across the countries of the Americas?") |>
  gf_labs(y = "country") |>
  gf_refine(scale_x_log10())
```

```{r}
#| label: main-character-question-C-violin

# Question 2
ggplot(C_mod, aes(continent, gdpPercap, colour = continent)) +
  geom_violin() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(title = "How does GDP per capita vary per country across the Americas?")
```

```{r}
#| label: main-character-question-C-boxplot

# Question 2
ggplot(C_mod, aes(continent, gdpPercap, colour = continent)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(title = "How does GDP per capita vary per country across the Americas?")
```

```{r}
#| label: question-3-lifeExp-vs-gdpPercap

# Question 3
ggplot(C_mod, aes(gdpPercap, lifeExp, colour = continent)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() + # decompress the points squashed on the left of the graph
  labs(title = "Are GDP per capita and life expectancy related?")

mosaic::cor.test(lifeExp ~ gdpPercap, data = C_mod) |> broom::tidy()
```

```{r}
#| label: maps-C

# Question 4
C_mod |> gf_sf(geometry = ~ geometry, fill = ~ pop, color = ~ continent,
        title = "Where do the most people live in the Americas?")
C_mod |> gf_sf(geometry = ~ geometry, fill = ~ lifeExp, color = ~ continent,
        title = "Where is life expectancy highest in the Americas?")
C_mod |> gf_sf(geometry = ~ geometry, fill = ~ gdpPercap, color = ~ continent,
        title = "Where is GDP per capita highest in the Americas?")
```

### 6. Say

~~Caption + one sentence we will stand behind.~~

1. Population is very uneven: the United States (about 301 million) and Brazil (about 190 million) are far bigger than everyone else, while the middle country has only about 9.3 million people.
1. Most countries of the Americas sit between about 5,700 and 12,000 dollars of `gdpPercap`. The box plot alone hides the story, but the jitter shows two countries far above the rest, the United States (42,952) and Canada (36,319), and one far below, Haiti (1,202).
1. Across the 25 countries of the Americas, `lifeExp` and `gdpPercap` are positively correlated (r = 0.59, p-value = 0.002). Haiti is the poorest country and also has the shortest life, at 60.9 years.
1. On the maps, the richest and longest-living countries are in the north (Canada and the United States). Our prediction was only half right: the biggest country is also the richest, but Brazil, the second biggest, is only in the middle for `gdpPercap`.

### 7. Limit

~~What this panel cannot do.~~

- It doesn't say *why* countries differ.
- It doesn't show change over TIME, since there is only 2007.
- It doesn't prove that money causes long life. Correlation is not causation.
- It only covers the Americas, so it cannot answer the "where in Africa" part of our spine.

# Panel D — Erin Brockovich

*Erin Brockovich in Hinkley, California: a hand-built plume of contaminated water and the homes of the families she met.*

### 1. See the table

~~What is a case? Which columns are Quant / Qual? What is missing?~~

First, a base map pointed at Hinkley, so we can check we are in the right place. `Esri.WorldImagery` is satellite, so the PG&E site, streets and houses show up at zoom 14.

```{r}
#| label: base-map-hinkley

leaflet() |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldImagery") |>
  setView(lng = -117.2050, lat = 34.9360, zoom = 14)
```

Tibble #1: the plume. Each row is one corner of the plume POLYGON. It starts at the PG&E tanks and runs about 1 mile southwards towards Hinkley.

```{r}
#| label: tibble-1-plume

plume <- tibble(
  lng = c(-117.2135, -117.2095, -117.2040, -117.2030, -117.2090, -117.2160, -117.2165),
  lat = c( 34.9460,   34.9460,   34.9380,   34.9270,   34.9230,   34.9290,   34.9390)
)
plume
```

Tibble #2: the families. Each row (case) is one family's home, as a POINT.

```{r}
#| label: tibble-2-families

families <- tibble(
  family = c("Jensen", "Robinson", "Irving", "Matthews", "Gomez"),
  address = c("12 Mountain View Rd", "40 Acacia St", "7 Summerset Rd",
              "88 Community Blvd", "25 Serra Rd"),
  phone = c("555-0101", "555-0102", "555-0103", "555-0104", "555-0105"),
  people = c(4, 3, 5, 2, 6),
  illness = c("Breast cancer", "Tumours", "Nosebleeds", "Headaches", "Rashes"),
  severity = c("High", "High", "Medium", "Low", "Medium"),
  water_from = c("Well", "Well", "Well", "Well", "Well"),
  signed_up = c("Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "No", "Yes"),
  col = c("red", "red", "orange", "yellow", "orange"),
  lng = c(-117.2100, -117.2075, -117.2120, -117.2060, -117.2135),
  lat = c( 34.9400,   34.9350,   34.9310,   34.9260,   34.9290)
)
families
```

My data has:

- `plume`: 7 rows and 2 columns. Each row is one corner of the plume.
- `families`: 5 rows and 11 columns. Each row is one family's home.
- `family`, `address`, `phone`: Qualitative, categorical. Encoded <chr>. One per family.
- `illness`: Qualitative, categorical. Encoded <chr>
- `severity`: Qualitative, ordinal ("Low" < "Medium" < "High"). Encoded <chr>
- `water_from`: Qualitative, categorical. Encoded <chr>. Every family drinks well water.
- `signed_up`: Qualitative, categorical ("Yes" / "No"). Did the family join the case against PG&E?
- `col`: the colour for each `severity`, used to colour the markers.
- `people`: Quantitative, numeric. How many people live in the home.
- `lng`, `lat`: Quantitative, numeric. Where the point is.

There is no missing data. Everything is made up by hand: the families, addresses, phone numbers and illnesses are hypothetical, and the coordinates are approximate.

### 2. Ask

~~One question *this* table can answer. One it cannot. Write both.~~

Possibly can answer:

1. Which families live on top of the plume, and how sick are they? (Main Character Question)

Possibly cannot answer:

1. Did the chromium in the water *cause* the illnesses? (No water tests or medical records)
1. How did the plume grow over the years? (One snapshot only)

### 3. Choose a mark

~~Geom, map mark, or (later) test that matches the pair type. Name it before you code.~~

1. Interactive map (`leaflet`): plume as `addPolygons()`, homes as `addCircleMarkers()` coloured by `severity`, with popups and a legend

### 4. Predict

~~What do we think we will see? One sentence, before Run.~~

I think the families closest to the PG&E tanks, in the middle of the plume, will have the most severe illnesses.

### 5. Make

~~Human brick first. Optional: one AI prompt, pasted below, only for what section 3 named.~~

**Which families live on top of the plume, and how sick are they?**

```{r}
#| label: main-character-question-D

# Question 1
popup <- paste(
  "<strong>", families$family, "</strong><br>",
  families$address, "<br>",
  "Phone: ", families$phone, "<br>",
  "People at home: ", families$people, "<br>",
  "Illness: ", families$illness, "<br>",
  "Severity: ", families$severity, "<br>",
  "Water from: ", families$water_from, "<br>",
  "Signed up: ", families$signed_up, "<br>"
)

leaflet(data = families) |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldImagery") |>
  setView(lng = -117.2050, lat = 34.9360, zoom = 14) |>
  # Tibble #1: the plume
  addPolygons(
    lng = plume$lng, lat = plume$lat,
    color = "purple", weight = 2,
    fill = TRUE, fillColor = "purple",
    popup = "Contaminated groundwater plume"
  ) |>
  # The PG&E tanks
  addMarkers(
    lng = -117.2115, lat = 34.9455,
    label = "PG&E compressor station (tanks)",
    labelOptions = labelOptions(noHide = TRUE, textOnly = FALSE, textsize = 14)
  ) |>
  # Tibble #2: the families, coloured by severity
  addCircleMarkers(
    lng = ~lng, lat = ~lat,
    radius = 8, # Pixels
    color = families$col,
    stroke = FALSE,
    fillOpacity = 1,
    label = families$family,
    popup = popup
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    title = "Illness severity",
    colors = c("red", "orange", "yellow"),
    labels = c("High", "Medium", "Low")
  )
```

### 6. Say

~~Caption + one sentence we will stand behind.~~

Every family on the map lives on top of the plume and drinks well water. The two families closest to the PG&E tanks, the Jensens and the Robinsons, have the most severe illnesses, while the Matthews family, at the far southern tip of the plume, has the mildest.

### 7. Limit

~~What this panel cannot do.~~

- It isn't proof that the chromium caused the illnesses.
- It doesn't speak for the whole town (only 5 made-up families).
- It doesn't show how the plume spread over TIME.

## Hunch 1: AI Belief Among Art and Design Students

*We collected data from across the Srishti Manipal campus. Our sample size for this was n = 60, which consisted of 30 art/BFA students and 30 design/BDes students, which included an equal number of boys and girls.*

### 1. See the table

~~What is a case? Which columns are Quant / Qual? What is missing?~~

```{r}
#| label: inspect-E-data-1

dplyr::glimpse(E)
```

My E data has:

- 60 observations and 4 variables. Each row (case) is one student.
- `count`: Quantitative, numeric. Just the student's number, 1 to 60, so we do not analyse it.
- `program`: Qualitative, categorical. Encoded <chr>, to be mutated
- `gender`: Qualitative, categorical. Encoded <chr>, to be mutated
- `AI_belief`: Qualitative, categorical. Encoded <chr>, to be mutated

```{r}
#| label: inspect-E-data-2

skimr::skim(E)
```

Furthermore, on the Qual variables E data has :

- `gender` has 2 levels: "boy" (30) and "girl" (30)
- `program` has 2 levels: "art" (30) and "design" (30)
- `AI_belief` also has 2 levels: "no" (32) and "yes" (28)

There is NO missing data. We are good to mutate.

```{r}
#| label: mutate-E-factors

AI <- E |>
  mutate(
    gender = as.factor(gender),
    program = as.factor(program),
    AI_belief = as.factor(AI_belief)
  )

glimpse(AI)
```

All ready now.

### 2. Ask

~~One question *this* table can answer. One it cannot. Write both.~~

Possibly can answer:

1. Do design students have greater belief in AI compared to art students? (Main Character Question)
1. Does it differ between boys and girls?

Possibly cannot answer:

1. *Why* do students believe in AI or not? (We only asked yes / no)

### 3. Choose a mark

~~Geom, map mark, or (later) test that matches the pair type. Name it before you code.~~

1. Mosaic Chart + Chi-Square Test

### 4. Predict

~~What do we think we will see? One sentence, before Run.~~

We think Design students are more likely to have a greater belief in AI compared to art students, and boys are more likely to have a greater belief than girls.

### 5. Make

~~Human brick first. Optional: one AI prompt, pasted below, only for what section 3 named.~~

```{r}
#| label: main-character-question-E-AI

# Question 1 and 2
vcd::structable(AI_belief ~ program + gender, data = AI) |>
  vcd::mosaic(shade = TRUE, main = "Do design students believe in AI more than art students? Boys more than girls?")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-E-program-test
#| tbl-cap: "AI Belief vs Program: Chi-Square Test"

# Question 1
mosaic::xchisq.test(AI_belief ~ program, data = AI)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-E-gender-test
#| tbl-cap: "AI Belief vs Gender: Chi-Square Test"

# Question 2
mosaic::xchisq.test(AI_belief ~ gender, data = AI)
```

### 6. Say

~~Caption + one sentence we will stand behind.~~

*Gender, not program, drives AI belief.*

1. Design students said yes a little more often than art students (16 of 30 vs 12 of 30), but the difference is not significant (X-squared = 0.60, p-value = 0.44).
1. Boys believe significantly more than girls (19 of 30 boys vs 9 of 30 girls said yes, X-squared = 5.42, p-value = 0.02), regardless of whether they study art or design.

### 7. Limit

~~What this panel cannot do.~~

"Belief" means something different to each student. One person might say yes because AI exists and they use it daily; another might say no because they're thinking about ethics or environmental cost.

```{r}
#| label: inspect-h4-data-2

skimr::skim(h4)
```

Furthermore, on the Qual variables h4 data has :

- `department` has 2 levels: SMI and MIT
- `relationship_status` has 2 levels: Yes and No

There is NO missing data. We are good to mutate.

```{r}
#| label: mutate-h4-factors

bfgf <- h4 |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))

glimpse(bfgf)
```

All ready now.

### 2. Ask

~~One question *this* table can answer. One it cannot. Write both.~~

Possibly can answer:

1. Are SMI (art and design) students more likely to be in a relationship than MIT (engineering) students? (Main Character Question)

Possibly cannot answer:

1. *Why* are some students in a relationship and others not? (We only asked yes / no)

### 3. Choose a mark

~~Geom, map mark, or (later) test that matches the pair type. Name it before you code.~~

1. Bar chart as proportions, Mosaic Chart + Chi-Square Test

### 4. Predict

~~What do we think we will see? One sentence, before Run.~~

SMI students are more likely to be in a relationship (or a situationship) than MIT students.

### 5. Make

~~Human brick first. Optional: one AI prompt, pasted below, only for what section 3 named.~~

```{r}
#| label: main-character-question-E-relationship

# Question 1
bfgf |> gf_bar(~ department, fill = ~ relationship_status, position = "fill") |>
  gf_labs(title = "Are SMI students more likely to be in a relationship than MIT students?",
          y = "Proportion of students")

vcd::structable(relationship_status ~ department, data = bfgf) |>
  vcd::mosaic(shade = TRUE, main = "Relationship status by department")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-h4-test
#| tbl-cap: "Relationship Status vs Department: Chi-Square Test"

# Question 1
mosaic::xchisq.test(relationship_status ~ department, data = bfgf)
```

### 6. Say

~~Caption + one sentence we will stand behind.~~

*The romantic art student is a myth, at least on our campus.*

12 SMI students and 13 MIT students said yes, almost identical. The test confirms there is no real difference (p = 1).

### 7. Limit

~~What this panel cannot do.~~

A one-person difference between 12 and 13 means nothing statistically. "Relationship" was also left undefined, so some students may have counted situationships and others may not.

## Hunch 5: Do Tattoos Make People Look More Attractive?

### 1. See the table

~~What is a case? Which columns are Quant / Qual? What is missing?~~

```{r}
#| label: inspect-h5-data-1

dplyr::glimpse(h5)
```

My h5 data has:

- 60 observations and 4 variables. Each row (case) is one student.
- `Respondents`: Quantitative, numeric. Just the student's number, so we do not analyse it.
- `Gender`: Qualitative, categorical. Encoded <chr>, to be mutated
- `` `Has_tattoos?` ``: Qualitative, categorical. Encoded <chr>, to be mutated
- `Opinion`: Qualitative, categorical. Encoded <chr>, to be mutated. Does this person find tattoos attractive?

```{r}

```

Furthermore, on the Qual variables h5 data has :

- `Gender` has 2 levels: M and F
- `Has_tattoos?` has 2 levels: yes and no
- `Opinion` has 2 levels: yes and no

There is NO missing data. The `?` in `Has_tattoos?` makes the name awkward to type, so we rename it to `Has_tattoos` while we mutate.

```{r}
#| label: mutate-h5-factors

tto <- h5 |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))

glimpse(tto)
```

All ready now.

### 2. Ask

~~One question *this* table can answer. One it cannot. Write both.~~

Possibly can answer:

1. Do people with tattoos find tattoos more attractive? (Main Character Question)
1. Does this differ by gender?

Possibly cannot answer:

1. *Which kind* of tattoo do people find attractive? (We only asked yes / no)

### 3. Choose a mark

~~Geom, map mark, or (later) test that matches the pair type. Name it before you code.~~

1. Bar chart as proportions, Mosaic Chart + Chi-Square Test

### 4. Predict

~~What do we think we will see? One sentence, before Run.~~

People with tattoos will find tattoos more attractive, and girls more than boys.

### 5. Make

~~Human brick first. Optional: one AI prompt, pasted below, only for what section 3 named.~~

```{r}
#| label: main-character-question-E-tattoos

# Question 1 and 2
tto |> gf_bar(~ Has_tattoos, fill = ~ Opinion, position = "fill") |>
  gf_facet_wrap(~ Gender) |>
  gf_labs(title = "Finds tattoos attractive, by tattoo status and gender",
          x = "Has a tattoo", y = "Proportion of students")

vcd::structable(Opinion ~ Has_tattoos + Gender, data = tto) |>
  vcd::mosaic(shade = TRUE, main = "Do people with tattoos find tattoos more attractive?")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-h5-test

```

### 6. Say

~~Caption + one sentence we will stand behind.~~

*Having a tattoo doesn't change what you think of them.*

Opinions on tattoo attractiveness are almost exactly the same across genders and between people with and without tattoos (p = 1 for both).

### 7. Limit

~~What this panel cannot do.~~

"Attractive" is a single yes/no, which hides nuance: someone may like small tattoos but not face tattoos. The sample is also just 60 students from one campus, so it can't stand in for young people in general.

## Hunch 6: TV Shows: Modern Family is the favourite.

### 1. See the table

~~What is a case? Which columns are Quant / Qual? What is missing?~~

```{r}
#| label: read-h6-data
#| warning: false

h6 <- readxl::read_excel("dataE/FOSEDA Panel E data.xlsx",
                         col_types = c("numeric", "date", "date", "date")) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

glimpse(h6) # Check what is happening
```

My h6 data has:

- 69 observations and 4 variables. Each row (case) is one student.
- `students`: Quantitative, numeric. Just the student's number.
- `friends`, `house`, `modern_family`: each student's score for that show. Excel stored the scores as dates <dttm>, so the score is hiding in the *day* of the date. We pull it out with `lubridate::day()`.

Then we `pivot_longer()` the three show columns into two: `show` (Qual) and `scores` (Quant), so that each row is one student's score for one show.

```{r}
#| label: mutate-h6-long

h6_mod <- h6 |>
  mutate(
    friends = lubridate::day(friends) |> as.numeric(),
    house = lubridate::day(house) |> as.numeric(),
    modern_family = lubridate::day(modern_family) |> as.numeric()
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(-students), names_to = "show", values_to = "scores") |>
  mutate(show = as.factor(show))

glimpse(h6_mod)
```

```{r}
#| label: inspect-h6-data-2

skimr::skim(h6_mod)
```

Furthermore, after the pivot h6_mod has :

- `show`: Qualitative, 3 levels: "friends", "house" and "modern_family"
- `scores`: Quantitative, numeric. Mean ___, sd ___, min ___, max ___ *(fill in from `skim()`)*

Missing data: YES. Many students had not watched or rated every show, especially House, so `scores` has ___ missing values. *(fill in from the `n_missing` column of `skim()`)* We drop them before the ANOVA.

```{r}
#| label: drop-h6-missing

tvshows_clean <- h6_mod |> filter(!is.na(scores))
```

All ready now.

### 2. Ask

~~One question *this* table can answer. One it cannot. Write both.~~

Possibly can answer:

1. Which show do students rate highest: Friends, House or Modern Family? (Main Character Question)
1. Which pairs of shows are rated differently?

Possibly cannot answer:

1. *Why* do students like one show more than another? (We only have a score)

### 3. Choose a mark

~~Geom, map mark, or (later) test that matches the pair type. Name it before you code.~~

1. Density plot, Box Plot + ANOVA
1. Pairwise comparison plot

### 4. Predict

~~What do we think we will see? One sentence, before Run.~~

Modern Family will be rated the highest of the three shows.

### 5. Make

~~Human brick first. Optional: one AI prompt, pasted below, only for what section 3 named.~~

```{r}
#| label: main-character-question-E-tvshows

# Question 1
tvshows_clean |> gf_density(~ scores, fill = ~ show, alpha = 0.5, title = "Which show do students rate highest?")

tvshows_clean |> gf_boxplot(scores ~ show, fill = ~ show, title = "Which show do students rate highest?")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-h6-anova
#| tbl-cap: "Scores vs Show: ANOVA"

# Question 1
aov(scores ~ show, data = tvshows_clean) |> supernova::supernova()
```

```{r}
#| label: h6-question-2

# Question 2
aov(scores ~ show, data = tvshows_clean) |> supernova::pairwise(plot = TRUE)
```

### 6. Say

~~Caption + one sentence we will stand behind.~~

Modern Family was rated the highest overall, as we predicted, with ratings clustering around 8-9, while House had the most spread with people either loving it or not. The ANOVA confirms these differences are real and not just chance (F = 8.44, p = 0.0004).

The pairwise comparison further revealed that Modern Family was rated significantly higher than both Friends and House. However, there was no statistically significant difference between Friends and House.

This suggests that Modern Family was the clear favourite among the students who rated these shows, supporting our hunch.

### 7. Limit

~~What this panel cannot do.~~

In this dataset, there were a lot of missing values (NA), since not many people had watched/rated House. In an ideal study, all the people within the sample should have watched all the shows, Friends, House and Modern Family.

# Conclusion

- **The question we will defend in ninety seconds:** Who arrives in acute coronary crisis, which habits travel with that crisis, and where is life short? Panels A and B answer the first two with the patients' bodies and habits, and Panel C shows that in the Americas, richer countries live longer (r = 0.59).
- **What we will not claim:** that smoking, obesity or cholesterol *cause* a crisis, that money *causes* long life, or that chromium *caused* the illnesses in Hinkley. Nothing here was an experiment.
- **Limits:** one snapshot in time, patients who already arrived in crisis, the Americas instead of Africa in Panel C, made-up families in Panel D, and small, self-reported campus samples (n = 60 to 69) in Panel E.
